preamble: Glottalization: a plain or aspirated velar stop [k] becomes the ejective [kʼ]. The best-known case is Ossetic, which, unusually for an Indo-European language, has a full ejective series (pʼ tʼ kʼ tsʼ tʃʼ). Ossetic ejectives are usually attributed to Kartvelian and/or Northeast Caucasian influence, and many occur in loans (e.g. Georgian კალათი > Ossetic къалати 'basket', with initial kʼ), where the ejective was already present. A handful of inherited Iranian words show k > kʼ: Proto-Iranian *darakā- > Iron дӕркъ 'heifer', *ni-kata- > никъӕд 'to carve', *káwfš > къупп 'hill'. Ossetic and Georgian also render Russian k in some loans as kʼ (word-initially in Ossetic къабуска, къафетт, къурткӕ). A plausible reason, not stated in the sources used, is that their plain voiceless stops are aspirated. In Cusco–Collao Quechua, ejectives (absent in Chanka/Ayacucho, which is a sister variety, not the ancestor) are thought to be innovations borrowed from Aymara after Proto-Quechua split up. Eastern Armenian dialects are reported to realise the Classical tenuis series as ejectives, but this is not part of the standard language. The PIE glottalic theory posits original ejectives, but it is a reconstruction hypothesis, not an attested shift, and is not counted here.
